Variable Handling in TaktX

General Concept: Variables in BPMN processes store data and state throughout process execution. In TaktX, variable handling is managed by the ScopeProcessor and Scope classes, ensuring robust scoping, isolation, and mapping between process elements.

Scoping Mechanism in TaktX

Each process instance, subprocess, and event subprocess in TaktX has its own variable scope. Scopes are organized hierarchically, forming a tree structure. Variables defined in a parent scope are visible to all child scopes (subprocesses, event subprocesses, etc.), but variables defined in a child scope are not visible to the parent or sibling scopes. This ensures data isolation and prevents accidental data leaks or overwrites.

  • Parent-to-Child Visibility: Child scopes can read and use variables from their parent scope.
  • Child-to-Parent Isolation: Parent scopes cannot access variables defined only in a child scope, unless those variables are explicitly mapped out.
  • Explicit Mapping: Input and output mappings (using FEEL expressions) control which variables are passed into or out of a scope.
  • Automatic Cleanup: When a scope ends, its local variables are cleaned up, ensuring no data leaks to other parts of the process.

BPMN Example: Variable Scoping Across Subprocess Levels

 

Example Explanation: In this example, the main process defines a variable orderId. The first subprocess ("Payment Subprocess") can access orderId and defines its own variable paymentStatus. A nested subprocess ("Fraud Check Subprocess") can access both orderId and paymentStatus, and defines fraudScore. When the nested subprocess ends, fraudScore is cleaned up unless explicitly mapped out. The parent subprocess and main process cannot access fraudScore unless it is mapped out. This demonstrates the hierarchical visibility and isolation of variables in TaktX.

Key Features:

  • Strict variable scoping for each process, subprocess, and event subprocess.
  • Input and output mappings using FEEL expressions.
  • Support for global, local, and transient variables.
  • Automatic cleanup of variables when a scope ends.
  • Isolation between parent and child scopes unless explicitly mapped.
